text: Introduction
trace: Contents --> Introduction

text: Current M-Plane specification mandates role-based access control with local user management. This implies that the Netconf Controller must keep track of locally defined users in each managed O-RU. It also means that some default behavior must be applied during installation of an O-RU, e.g. default users pre-defined by vendor for SSH and first trusted user connecting over TLS is given "sudo" role.
trace: Contents --> Introduction

text: In this technical report key security issues due to locally defined users in each managed O-RU are analyzed. The option of using a centralized user management is also evaluated, and solutions proposed along with the necessary security requirements.

text: 4 Background

text: 4.1 Netconf Access Control
trace: 2 References --> 4 Background --> 4.1 Netconf Access Control

text: Netconf access control is defined in the WG4 M-Plane Specification \[i.2\] to be used in the O-RU, but only with local user management configuration in each O-RU.
trace: 2 References --> 4 Background --> 4.1 Netconf Access Control

text: Netconf access control is also used on the O1 interface. The WG11 Security Requirements and Controls Specification \[i.1\] defines, for O1 entities, that \(REQ-NAC-FUN-9\): Netconf endpoints SHALL support external user to group mapping via at least one of the following protocols: LDAP with StartTLS, OAuth 2.0, RADIUS with EAP, and TACACS/TACACS+.
trace: 2 References --> 4 Background --> 4.1 Netconf Access Control

text: 4.2 Software and Configuration Server \(SCS\)
trace: 2 References --> 4.2 Software and Configuration Server \(SCS\)

text: The 3GPP TS 28.314 \[i.3\] and TS 28.315 \[i.4\] describes the SCS as an entity and how it can be used in a Plug and Connect use case to provide initial configuration to a Network Element. The O-RU can be seen as a Network Element that during the provisioning needs to get configuration and find an O-RU controller.
trace: 2 References --> 4.2 Software and Configuration Server \(SCS\)

text: The 3GPP TS 28.316 \[i.5\] describes how a Network Element can get the address to an SCS from a DHCP server.
trace: 2 References --> 4.2 Software and Configuration Server \(SCS\)

text: The WG4 M-Plane Specification \[i.2\] clause on "Start-up installation" currently does not include the use of an SCS.

text: 5 Key Issues
trace: 2 References --> 5 Key Issues

text: This clause details the key issues identified for security aspects related to user management in the O-RU.
trace: 2 References --> 5 Key Issues

text: 5.1 Key Issue \#1: Default account in O-RU
trace: 2 References --> 5 Key Issues --> 5.1 Key Issue \#1: Default account in O-RU

text: 5.1.1 Key issue detail
trace: 2 References --> 5 Key Issues --> 5.1 Key Issue \#1: Default account in O-RU --> 5.1.1 Key issue detail

text: Current M-plane specification \[i.2\] requires a vendor specific default account. Default accounts should be avoided if possible.
trace: 2 References --> 5 Key Issues --> 5.1 Key Issue \#1: Default account in O-RU --> 5.1.1 Key issue detail

text: The 3GPP TS 33.117 \[i.8\] section 4.2.3.4.2.2 states that predefined accounts shall be deleted or disabled. "Should this  measure not be possible the accounts shall be locked for remote login".
trace: 2 References --> 5 Key Issues --> 5.1 Key Issue \#1: Default account in O-RU --> 5.1.1 Key issue detail

text: 5.1.2 Security threats
trace: 2 References --> 5 Key Issues --> 5.1 Key Issue \#1: Default account in O-RU --> 5.1.2 Security threats

text:
* An attacker can log on to the O-RU in these cases: The vendor defined default account \(username/password\) is leaked.
  * Any entity that is connecting using an accepted certificate using 
    * o any operator-signed certificate verified by an installed trust anchor or
    * o any certificate if the enrollment failed and the O-RU supports the optional feature of using its preinstalled vendor-signed certificate for setting up mTLS connections to its O-RU Controller\(s\) \(see \[i.2\], clause 6.2.6.3\), as in this case the O-RU does not have an installed trust anchor.
trace: 2 References --> 5 Key Issues --> 5.1 Key Issue \#1: Default account in O-RU --> 5.1.2 Security threats

text: An attacker can use a successful log-on to connect to the O-RU before the connection to the O-RU controller is established. New accounts can be created.
trace: 2 References --> 5 Key Issues --> 5.1 Key Issue \#1: Default account in O-RU --> 5.1.2 Security threats

text: If the default account is not being disabled, it can be used to connect and modify existing configuration.
trace: 2 References --> 5 Key Issues --> 5.1 Key Issue \#1: Default account in O-RU --> 5.1.2 Security threats

text: 5.1.3 Potential security requirements
trace: 2 References --> 5 Key Issues --> 5.1 Key Issue \#1: Default account in O-RU --> 5.1.3 Potential security requirements

text: To mitigate the threat of an attacker using a default account to create additional accounts, the O-RU controller can verify that no unwanted accounts exist. This can be done every time when the O-RU Controller connects to an O-RU by comparing the O-RU user account configuration with the planned settings. An alternative is to avoid using a default account and rely on centralized user management during provisioning.
trace: 2 References --> 5 Key Issues --> 5.1 Key Issue \#1: Default account in O-RU --> 5.1.3 Potential security requirements

text: 5.2 Key Issue \#2: Default account get sudo role
trace: 2 References --> 5 Key Issues --> 5.2 Key Issue \#2: Default account get sudo role

text: 5.2.1 Key issue detail
trace: 2 References --> 5 Key Issues --> 5.2.1 Key issue detail

text: Current M-plane specification requires that when first connection is made, the first \(i.e. default\) user get sudo role by default. Default accounts should be avoided if possible.
trace: 2 References --> 5 Key Issues --> 5.2.1 Key issue detail

text: 5.2.2 Security threats
trace: 2 References --> 5.2.2 Security threats

text: The security threats identified with first connected user getting sudo role:
trace: 2 References --> 5.2.2 Security threats
2 References --> 5.2.2 Security threats
2 References --> 5.2.2 Security threats
2 References --> 5.2.2 Security threats

text: An Attacker can connect using
trace: 2 References --> 5.2.2 Security threats

text:
* any operator-signed certificate verified by an installed trust anchor or
  * any certificate if the enrollment failed and the O-RU supports the optional feature of using its pre-installed vendor-signed certificate for setting up mTLS connections to its O-RU Controller\(s\) \(see \[i.2\], clause 6.2.6.3\), as in this case the O-RU does not have an installed trust anchor or
  * a leaked default username/password
trace: 2 References --> 5.2.2 Security threats

text: will get "sudo" role. This can be used to connect to the O-RU before the connection to the O-RU controller is established. New accounts can be created.
trace: 2 References --> 5.2.2 Security threats

text: If the default account is not disabled, it can also be used after the connection to the O-RU controller is established to connect and modify existing configuration.
trace: 2 References --> 5.2.2 Security threats

text: 5.2.3 Potential security requirements
trace: 2 References --> 5.2.2 Security threats --> 5.2.3 Potential security requirements

text: To mitigate the threat of an attacker using a default account, get "sudo" role and creates additional accounts, the O-RU controller can verify that no unwanted accounts exist. An alternative is to avoid using a default account and rely on centralized user management during provisioning.
trace: 2 References --> 5.2.2 Security threats --> 5.2.3 Potential security requirements

text: 5.3 Key Issue \#3: The O-RU controller must keep track of locally defined users in each managed O-RU
trace: 2 References --> 5.3 Key Issue \#3: The O-RU controller must keep track of locally defined users in each managed O-RU

text: 5.3.1 Key issue detail
trace: 2 References --> 5.3 Key Issue \#3: The O-RU controller must keep track of locally defined users in each managed O-RU --> 5.3.1 Key issue detail

text: Current M-plane specification defines role-based access control configured in each O-RU. Allowing for centralized user management would simplify management.
trace: 2 References --> 5.3 Key Issue \#3: The O-RU controller must keep track of locally defined users in each managed O-RU --> 5.3.1 Key issue detail

text: 5.3.2 Security threats
trace: 2 References --> 5.3.2 Security threats

text: The security threats identified with only local user management in O-RU, configured by the O-RU controller:
trace: 2 References --> 5.3.2 Security threats

text: • If the same user configuration is used in all O-RUs, any O-RU controller can connect to any O-RU. Changes will have to be performed on every O-RU.
trace: 2 References --> 5.3.2 Security threats

text: 5.3.3 Potential security requirements
trace: 2 References --> 5.3.2 Security threats --> 5.3.3 Potential security requirements

text: To simplify management a centralized user management system can be used.
trace: 2 References --> 5.3.2 Security threats --> 5.3.3 Potential security requirements

text: 5.4 Key Issue \#4: How to get initial configuration to Central Server?
trace: 2 References --> 5.4 Key Issue \#4: How to get initial configuration to Central Server?

text: 5.4.1 Key issue detail
trace: 2 References --> 5.4 Key Issue \#4: How to get initial configuration to Central Server? --> 5.4.1 Key issue detail

text: When the O-RU is started for the first time, it will not have any operator specific configuration on how to connect to the central server. To use centralized user management this configuration is required.
trace: 2 References --> 5.4 Key Issue \#4: How to get initial configuration to Central Server? --> 5.4.1 Key issue detail
2 References --> 5.4 Key Issue \#4: How to get initial configuration to Central Server? --> 5.4.1 Key issue detail
2 References --> 5.4 Key Issue \#4: How to get initial configuration to Central Server? --> 5.4.1 Key issue detail
2 References --> 5.4 Key Issue \#4: How to get initial configuration to Central Server? --> 5.4.1 Key issue detail

text: 5.4.2 Security threats
trace: 2 References --> 5.4 Key Issue \#4: How to get initial configuration to Central Server? --> 5.4.1 Key issue detail --> 5.4.2 Security threats

text: The security threats identified with the O-RU not having any operator specific configuration to use centralized user management:
trace: 2 References --> 5.4 Key Issue \#4: How to get initial configuration to Central Server? --> 5.4.1 Key issue detail --> 5.4.2 Security threats

text: • If the O-RU does not know the address to the Central AA server \(e.g. LDAP\) it will revert to the use of locally defined users, i.e. issue 1-3
trace: 2 References --> 5.4 Key Issue \#4: How to get initial configuration to Central Server? --> 5.4.1 Key issue detail --> 5.4.2 Security threats

text: 5.4.3 Potential security requirements
trace: 2 References --> 5.4 Key Issue \#4: How to get initial configuration to Central Server? --> 5.4.1 Key issue detail --> 5.4.3 Potential security requirements

text: The O-RU can get this data from one of the entities that it connects to during provisioning, i.e. DHCP, DNS and RA/CA, or from a new entity, e.g. SCS.
trace: 2 References --> 5.4 Key Issue \#4: How to get initial configuration to Central Server? --> 5.4.1 Key issue detail --> 5.4.3 Potential security requirements

text: 5.5 Key Issue \#5: How does the O-RU connect securely to the Central Server?
trace: 2 References --> 5.5 Key Issue \#5: How does the O-RU connect securely to the Central Server?

text: 5.5.1 Key issue detail
trace: 2 References --> 5.5 Key Issue \#5: How does the O-RU connect securely to the Central Server? --> 5.5.1 Key issue detail

text: The O-RU must have options to connect securely to the central server.
trace: 2 References --> 5.5 Key Issue \#5: How does the O-RU connect securely to the Central Server? --> 5.5.1 Key issue detail

text: 5.5.2 Security threats
trace: 2 References --> 5.5 Key Issue \#5: How does the O-RU connect securely to the Central Server? --> 5.5.2 Security threats

text: The security threats identified with O-RU not having a secure connection to the centralized user management server:
trace: 2 References --> 5.5 Key Issue \#5: How does the O-RU connect securely to the Central Server? --> 5.5.2 Security threats

text:
* Without a secure connection, the Central AA server \(e.g. LDAP\) can be fake
  * Without a secure connection, the transferred response from the central AA server can be tampered
trace: 2 References --> 5.5 Key Issue \#5: How does the O-RU connect securely to the Central Server? --> 5.5.2 Security threats

text: 5.5.3 Potential security requirements
trace: 2 References --> 5.5 Key Issue \#5: How does the O-RU connect securely to the Central Server? --> 5.5.3 Potential security requirements

text: The connection to the centralized server should be authenticated and should be confidentiality and integrity protected.
trace: 2 References --> 5.5 Key Issue \#5: How does the O-RU connect securely to the Central Server? --> 5.5.3 Potential security requirements

text: 5.6 Key Issue \#6: Availability of the centralized user management server for the O-RUs
trace: 2 References --> 5.6 Key Issue \#6: Availability of the centralized user management server for the O-RUs

text: 5.6.1 Key issue detail
trace: 2 References --> 5.6 Key Issue \#6: Availability of the centralized user management server for the O-RUs --> 5.6.1 Key issue detail

text: The centralized user management server should be available at all times. Hence the need to cover the below aspects
trace: 2 References --> 5.6 Key Issue \#6: Availability of the centralized user management server for the O-RUs --> 5.6.1 Key issue detail

text:
* Overloading of centralized server 
    * o Number of RUs connected to the server
    * o Frequency of making Authentication and Authorization calls
    * o Number of users that are managed centrally for the O-RU
  * Network connectivity 
    * o Connectivity loss between the O-RU and centralized server
  * SW/HW failure of centralized server
trace: 2 References --> 5.6 Key Issue \#6: Availability of the centralized user management server for the O-RUs --> 5.6.1 Key issue detail
2 References --> 5.6 Key Issue \#6: Availability of the centralized user management server for the O-RUs --> 5.6.1 Key issue detail
2 References --> 5.6 Key Issue \#6: Availability of the centralized user management server for the O-RUs --> 5.6.1 Key issue detail
2 References --> 5.6 Key Issue \#6: Availability of the centralized user management server for the O-RUs --> 5.6.1 Key issue detail

text: o The centralized server might be unavailable due to a software or HW failure and hence needs to be highly available
trace: 2 References --> 5.6 Key Issue \#6: Availability of the centralized user management server for the O-RUs --> 5.6.1 Key issue detail

text: 5.6.2 Security threats
trace: 2 References --> 5.6 Key Issue \#6: Availability of the centralized user management server for the O-RUs --> 5.6.2 Security threats

text:
* Slow response of the centralized server due to overloading
  * Unavailability of the centralized server due to overloading
  * No response due to network disconnection
  * No response due to SW/HW failure of the centralized server
trace: 2 References --> 5.6 Key Issue \#6: Availability of the centralized user management server for the O-RUs --> 5.6.2 Security threats

text: 5.6.3 Potential security requirements
trace: 2 References --> 5.6 Key Issue \#6: Availability of the centralized user management server for the O-RUs --> 5.6.3 Potential security requirements

text:
* Load model to be defined to ensure no overloading of the centralized server
  * Reliable connectivity between the O-RU and the centralized server
  * High availability of the centralized server
  * In case the connectivity to the central server is not available, local users to be activated and used until the connectivity is resolved
trace: 2 References --> 5.6 Key Issue \#6: Availability of the centralized user management server for the O-RUs --> 5.6.3 Potential security requirements

text: 5.7 Key Issue \#7: Categorisation of users that need to centrally and locally managed
trace: 2 References --> 5.7 Key Issue \#7: Categorisation of users that need to centrally and locally managed

text: 5.7.1 Key issue detail
trace: 2 References --> 5.7 Key Issue \#7: Categorisation of users that need to centrally and locally managed --> 5.7.1 Key issue detail

text: The purpose of centralized user management is to have effective administration and accountability of O-RU users. It is recommended that the users of the O-RU are being categorized into central and local users to ensure that centrally administered users are kept at a maximum and local users are at a minimum with a well defined need.
trace: 2 References --> 5.7 Key Issue \#7: Categorisation of users that need to centrally and locally managed --> 5.7.1 Key issue detail

text: 5.7.2 Security threats
trace: 2 References --> 5.7.2 Security threats

text: • O-RU user information could be mismanaged, classifying users managed centralized as local users, defeating the purpose of central authentication, authorization and administration.
trace: 2 References --> 5.7.2 Security threats

text: 5.7.3 Potential security requirements
trace: 2 References --> 5.7.3 Potential security requirements

text:
* Categorisation of central and local users for the O-RU
  * Minimise the usage of local users and maximise the usage of central users
trace: 2 References --> 5.7.3 Potential security requirements

text: When a user connects to a O-RU, first check if the user exists in central server, if no user found then check locally
trace: 2 References --> 5.7.3 Potential security requirements
2 References --> 5.7.3 Potential security requirements
2 References --> 5.7.3 Potential security requirements
2 References --> 5.7.3 Potential security requirements

text: 5.8 Key Issue \#8: Fetching initial security configuration data from a Software and Configuration Server
trace: 2 References --> 5.8 Key Issue \#8: Fetching initial security configuration data from a Software and Configuration Server

text: 5.8.1 Key issue detail
trace: 2 References --> 5.8 Key Issue \#8: Fetching initial security configuration data from a Software and Configuration Server --> 5.8.1 Key issue detail

text: The SCS is a server that can provide initial configuration data to an O-RU before first connection to an O-RU Controller similar to what is described in 3GPP TS 28.314 \[9\] and TS 28.315 \[10\]. The O-RU can get the address to the SCS from the DHCP server.
trace: 2 References --> 5.8 Key Issue \#8: Fetching initial security configuration data from a Software and Configuration Server --> 5.8.1 Key issue detail

text: The initial configuration data can be security related data such as the address to a central AA server, trusted certificates etc.
trace: 2 References --> 5.8 Key Issue \#8: Fetching initial security configuration data from a Software and Configuration Server --> 5.8.1 Key issue detail

text: 5.8.2 Security threats
trace: 2 References --> 5.8 Key Issue \#8: Fetching initial security configuration data from a Software and Configuration Server --> 5.8.2 Security threats

text: The security threats identified with O-RU fetching initial configuration from SCS:
trace: 2 References --> 5.8 Key Issue \#8: Fetching initial security configuration data from a Software and Configuration Server --> 5.8.2 Security threats

text:
* Without a secure connection, the SCS can be fake.
  * Without a secure connection, the configuration data can be tampered with in transit.
  * Without trust information, e.g. a trusted certificate, the O-RU cannot verify that the SCS is ok. This is however the same risk as the O-RU has with the O-RU Controller in current specification.
trace: 2 References --> 5.8 Key Issue \#8: Fetching initial security configuration data from a Software and Configuration Server --> 5.8.2 Security threats

text: 5.8.3 Potential security requirements
trace: 2 References --> 5.8 Key Issue \#8: Fetching initial security configuration data from a Software and Configuration Server --> 5.8.3 Potential security requirements

text: The connection to the SCS server that can provide initial configuration data to an O-RU should be authenticated and should be confidentiality and integrity protected.
trace: 2 References --> 5.8 Key Issue \#8: Fetching initial security configuration data from a Software and Configuration Server --> 5.8.3 Potential security requirements

text: 5.9 Key Issue \#9: Secure transport to the centralized authentication server
trace: 2 References --> 5.9 Key Issue \#9: Secure transport to the centralized authentication server

text: 5.9.1 Key issue detail
trace: 2 References --> 5.9 Key Issue \#9: Secure transport to the centralized authentication server --> 5.9.1 Key issue detail

text: Data in transit can be intercepted between the O-RU and the central server. From this perspective, there should be options of secure transport for the reason that credentials will be shared for authentication and authorization purposes which should not be compromised. There is a possibility to also have a compromised central server.

text: 5.9.2 Security threats

text: 5.10 Key Issue \#10: Secure storage of O-RU credentials
trace: 2 References --> 5.9 Key Issue \#9: Secure transport to the centralized authentication server --> 5.10 Key Issue \#10: Secure storage of O-RU credentials

text: 5.10.1 Key issue detail
trace: 2 References --> 5.9 Key Issue \#9: Secure transport to the centralized authentication server --> 5.10 Key Issue \#10: Secure storage of O-RU credentials --> 5.10.1 Key issue detail

text: Improper or missing controls for protection of security credentials at rest, generated by O-RAN components, may not allow a correct and rapid audit in case of a security incident occurrence. Security restoration is delayed. Missing availability and integrity of security credentials could lead to delays, wrong results, delays in security restoration and threat persistence \(\[i.1\] §5.4.1.1\). A secure mechanism for storing the credentials of the O-RU in the central server should be required. The credentials of the O-RU could be
trace: 2 References --> 5.9 Key Issue \#9: Secure transport to the centralized authentication server --> 5.10 Key Issue \#10: Secure storage of O-RU credentials --> 5.10.1 Key issue detail

text:
* Username and password
  * Certificates
  * Tokens
trace: 2 References --> 5.9 Key Issue \#9: Secure transport to the centralized authentication server --> 5.10 Key Issue \#10: Secure storage of O-RU credentials --> 5.10.1 Key issue detail

text: 5.10.2 Security threats
trace: 2 References --> 5.9 Key Issue \#9: Secure transport to the centralized authentication server --> 5.10.2 Security threats

text: • O-RU related credentials could be compromised by an attacker if the storage is not secure. The important aspect is that as all the data is stored centrally and the entire network could be potentially sabotaged if not secured. \(\[i.1\] T-O-RAN-06\).
trace: 2 References --> 5.9 Key Issue \#9: Secure transport to the centralized authentication server --> 5.10.2 Security threats

trace: 2 References --> 5.10.3 Potential security requirements

text: Secure mechanism of storing various types of credentials of the O-RU
trace: 2 References --> 5.10.3 Potential security requirements

text:
* Management of username and password centrally with salting mechanisms and a one-way hash
  * Certificates centrally managed with respect to users encompassing the life cycle management of enrollment, renewal and revocation.
  * Tokens created centrally in OAuth server and encrypted during motion and refreshing actions

text: 6 Mitigations and Solutions
trace: 6 Mitigations and Solutions

text: 6.1 Key Issue Analysis
trace: 6 Mitigations and Solutions --> 6.1 Key Issue Analysis

text: The 10 identified Key Issues can be grouped into these groups, Local User Management issues, Initial Provisioning, and Central Server Issues.
trace: 6 Mitigations and Solutions --> 6.1 Key Issue Analysis

text: The Local User Management Issues can be mitigated by using a Centralized User Management Service, however that means that the other two groups of issues come into play.
trace: 6 Mitigations and Solutions --> 6.1 Key Issue Analysis

text: The Key Issues with Initial Provisioning of data needed to securely connect to the central AA server can be mitigated by the services proposed for distributing Trust Anchors, i.e. Voucher based protocols, BRSKI based or SCS based solutions. It is concluded that DHCP, DNS and RA/CA methods would either not be secure or have the same Initial Provisioning issues.
trace: 6 Mitigations and Solutions --> 6.1 Key Issue Analysis

text: The Key Issues related to the Central AA server can be mitigated by placing security requirements on the Central AA server itself. This is however not a component designed by the O-RAN Alliance specifications so only recommendations can be made to the operators.
trace: 6 Mitigations and Solutions --> 6.1 Key Issue Analysis

text: 6.2 Solution \#1: Centralized User Management
trace: 6 Mitigations and Solutions --> 6.1 Key Issue Analysis --> 6.2 Solution \#1: Centralized User Management

text: To mitigate the listed Key Issues related to Local User Management it is proposed to allow the use of centralized user management services. There are many protocols to choose from and the investigation done on this topic before setting requirements on O1, showed that it was not possible to agree on one single protocol. It is proposed to allow the same protocols on the O-RU as on the O1 entities.
trace: 6 Mitigations and Solutions --> 6.1 Key Issue Analysis --> 6.2 Solution \#1: Centralized User Management

text: NOTE: An enquiry to companies participating in WG11 meetings resulted in a change proposal towards the O1 requirement where LDAP with StartTLS was selected as the primary choice of protocol. Proposed requirement:
trace: 6 Mitigations and Solutions --> 6.1 Key Issue Analysis --> 6.2 Solution \#1: Centralized User Management

text: REQ-x The O-RU MAY support external user-to-groupmapping with the role based access control concept.
trace: 6 Mitigations and Solutions --> 6.1 Key Issue Analysis --> 6.2 Solution \#1: Centralized User Management

text: Proposed security controls:
trace: 6 Mitigations and Solutions --> 6.1 Key Issue Analysis --> 6.2 Solution \#1: Centralized User Management

text: CTL-y An O-RU that supports external user to group mapping should support LDAP with StartTLS, and may also support OAuth 2.0, RADIUS with EAP, and TACACS/TACACS+.
trace: 6 Mitigations and Solutions --> 6.1 Key Issue Analysis --> 6.2 Solution \#1: Centralized User Management

text: CTL-z The centralized server may be an external 3rd party system or within the ORAN reside within a SMO or O-DU \(depending on hierarchical or hybrid mode\).
trace: 6 Mitigations and Solutions --> 6.1 Key Issue Analysis --> 6.2 Solution \#1: Centralized User Management

text: CTL-zz The centralized server stores the necessary credentials for the O-RU in a secure manner with access control \(mapping to KI10\)
trace: 6 Mitigations and Solutions --> 6.1 Key Issue Analysis --> 6.2 Solution \#1: Centralized User Management

text: CTL-zx An O-RU that supports external user to group mapping may support SAML and OIDC.
trace: 6 Mitigations and Solutions --> 6.1 Key Issue Analysis --> 6.2 Solution \#1: Centralized User Management

text: 6.3 Solution 2\#: Initial Provisioning
trace: 6 Mitigations and Solutions --> 6.3 Solution 2\#: Initial Provisioning

text: To mitigate the listed Key Issues related to Initial Provisioning of data needed to securely connect to the central AA server it is possible to use the already defined security control \[i.1\]:
trace: 6 Mitigations and Solutions --> 6.3 Solution 2\#: Initial Provisioning

text: SEC-CTL-TAP-5: An O-RAN PNF may support 3GPP SCS \[66\], \[67\], \[68\] for download of initial security configuration.
trace: 6 Mitigations and Solutions --> 6.3 Solution 2\#: Initial Provisioning

text: 6.4 Solution \#3 High Availability
trace: 6 Mitigations and Solutions --> 6.3 Solution 2\#: Initial Provisioning --> 6.4 Solution \#3 High Availability

text: To mitigate the listed Key Issues related to the use of a Centralized Authentication and Authorization Server it is proposed to recommend operators to plan the deployment with high availability.
